title: The Flannan Isles Mystery: Where Did 3 Lighthouse Keepers Go?
subject: flannan
description:
What do you think made Donald McArthur run out without his coat? 👇

In December 1900, three keepers vanished from a new lighthouse on Eilean Mòr, a rock twenty miles west of the Isle of Lewis. This case file follows the relief ship that found the station empty, Superintendent Robert Muirhead's report on the wrecked west landing, the logbook entries that turned out to be fiction, and the explanation most researchers accept today.

Sources: National Records of Scotland (Northern Lighthouse Board records NLC3/1/1, including Muirhead's report of 8 January 1901); Royal Museums Greenwich; Skeptoid #610 and Mike Dash's research for Fortean Studies and Fortean Times; Wikipedia, "Flannan Isles Lighthouse" and its references.

scenes.text: "The lamp was cleaned. The fountain full. Blinds on the windows." Someone chalked those words on a slate in a lighthouse on a lonely Atlantic rock, on the morning of the 15th of December, 1900.
Eleven days later, a ship arrived with the relief keeper. The lamp was still trimmed and ready. The kitchen was clean. The slate was still there.
The three men who were meant to be keeping that light were gone, and the sea around the island never gave back a single trace of them.
Over the next century, writers added stopped clocks, a half-eaten meal and a diary full of fear. Much of that was simply invented.
What survives in Scotland's national archives is plainer: a superintendent's report, a few letters, and a staff register with one word written beside two names in red ink.
Those papers describe one of the best known disappearances in British maritime history, the vanishing of the three keepers of the Flannan Isles.
The Flannan Isles are a small group of islands about twenty miles west of the Isle of Lewis, in Scotland's Outer Hebrides. Sailors called them the Seven Hunters.
The largest is Eilean Mòr, the Big Island, about thirty-eight acres of grass and rock, rising out of the sea on high cliffs.
The Northern Lighthouse Board built a light there in the late 1890s, designed by David Alan Stevenson, of the famous Scottish family of lighthouse engineers.
Every stone had to be hauled up the cliffs from small boats. The light was first lit on the 7th of December, 1899.
Three keepers lived on the rock at a time, while a fourth took his turn ashore at Breasclete, on Lewis, where the board kept houses for their families.
In December 1900, the principal keeper was James Ducat, forty-four years old, who had joined the lighthouse service twenty-two years earlier.
His assistant was Thomas Marshall, a former seaman. The third man, Donald McArthur, was an occasional keeper, filling in for an assistant named William Ross, who was off sick.
Ducat had a wife and four children on shore. The youngest, Arthur, was six. McArthur had a wife and two children. Marshall was unmarried.
The keeper on shore that month was Joseph Moore. He was due back on the island on the 20th of December. The weather kept him away for six more days.
Around midnight on the 15th of December, the steamer Archtor, bound from Philadelphia to Leith, passed the Flannans in bad weather. Her crew looked for the light. There was none.
The sighting was reported when the ship reached port, but it never reached the lighthouse commissioners in time. The letter passing it on is dated the 28th of December.
At about noon on the 26th, the lighthouse tender Hesperus finally reached Eilean Mòr. Captain James Harvie expected to see the keepers waiting at the landing. No one was there.
The crew sounded the whistle and fired a rocket. When nothing moved, Joseph Moore was put ashore alone, climbed the long stairway to the lighthouse, and found nobody inside.
He went back down, then returned with the buoymaster and two seamen. Together they searched the tower, the living quarters and the rest of the island.
The lamps had been trimmed and filled, the lens and machinery cleaned, the kitchen tidied. Two sets of outdoor clothing were missing.
Moore later said the kitchen utensils were all very clean, which to him meant the men had gone out some time after dinner.
That afternoon, Captain Harvie sent a telegram to the board in Edinburgh. It began with the words, "A dreadful accident has happened at the Flannans."
On the 29th of December, Superintendent Robert Muirhead arrived on the island. He had recruited all three of the missing men himself.
He began with the records. The last entries in the station log were for the 13th of December. Notes for the 14th and the morning of the 15th were still on the slate.
The light had been lit on the 14th and put out the next morning. The men had vanished, it seemed, on the afternoon of Saturday the 15th.
Then Muirhead walked to the west landing, one of two places on the island where a boat could come in. Some of the damage there, he wrote, was difficult to believe unless actually seen.
Iron railings around the crane platform were displaced and twisted. A block of stone weighing more than a ton had been torn out of place.
A box of ropes and gear, stored high above the landing, had been smashed open. Turf was stripped from the cliff top, some two hundred feet up.
A lifebuoy tied to the railings was gone. Muirhead reasoned that the sea had torn it off its ropes, even at that great height, a hundred and ten feet above sea level.
Back in the lighthouse, there was one more clue. Hanging indoors was a set of oilskins that belonged to Donald McArthur.
Moore told the superintendent that the keepers wore their heavy gear only when going down to the landings. Ducat's sea boots and waterproof were gone. So were Marshall's boots and oilskins.
McArthur's coat had stayed behind. Muirhead concluded that he had left the lighthouse in his shirt sleeves, in heavy rain, in the middle of a Hebridean winter.
It suggested a man in a hurry. It also broke the rules, which said the light must never be left with nobody inside.
No bodies were ever found. The men were simply gone, and with them any chance of learning what they had seen that afternoon.
The accounts of the visit do not fully agree. Harvie's telegram said the clocks had stopped. The notes drawn from Moore's own report describe everything indoors as being as it should be.
In the board's register of lightkeepers, beside the names of Ducat and Marshall, a clerk wrote one word in red ink: Disappeared, on or about the 15th of December, 1900.
At Carloway, on Lewis, the death register gave the cause as probably drowning. The word probably left room, and other people soon began to fill it.
In 1912, the poet Wilfrid Wilson Gibson published a ballad called Flannan Isle. In it, the searchers find a chair knocked over and a meal left uneaten on the table.
Neither detail appears in the official papers. Even so, later retellings repeated the poet's scene as if it had been reported by the men from the Hesperus.
Then came the logbook. Decades later, entries said to be Marshall's began to appear in print: a terrible storm, Ducat very quiet, McArthur crying.
The last entry, supposedly from the 15th of December, read: "Storm ended, sea calm. God is over all." None of it was in the official file.
The researcher Mike Dash went back to the sources for Fortean Times and concluded the entries were fiction, added long after the event. The real logbook has never been found.
Without that diary, the wilder ideas lost most of their support: a sea serpent, foreign spies, a planned escape by boat, or a curse on the old island.
One darker theory held that McArthur, said to be quick tempered, fought with the others near the cliff edge. Beyond his reputation, there is no evidence that any fight took place.
The explanation most researchers favour is far less dramatic, and it begins with a small fine handed to Thomas Marshall: five shillings.
According to research by James Love, Marshall had once been fined five shillings after equipment at the west landing was washed away in a storm.
If heavy seas were building that Saturday afternoon, Ducat and Marshall may have pulled on their boots and oilskins and gone down to secure the stores before they were lost again.
McArthur, up at the lighthouse, may have seen a larger wave coming that they could not, and run out without his coat to warn them or to help.
The landing lies at the head of a narrow inlet, with a cave below it. Researchers have argued that waves forced into that gap can surge far above the level of the open sea.
Walter Aldebert, principal keeper there in the 1950s, described repeated rogue waves at the landing, and said that one of them nearly took him as well.
In January 1901, Muirhead reached the same conclusion: an extra large sea had rushed up the face of the rock, gone above the men, and carried them away.
It fits the damage, the missing oilskins and the coat left on its peg. It still rests on a guess about what three men did on an afternoon nobody else saw.
On the morning of the 15th, one of them wrote that the lamp was cleaned, the fountain full, the blinds on the windows. Those were the last ordinary words the three keepers left.
